content.summary: Guidance on pre-hospital and network organization for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and initial emergency care for acute coronary syndromes (ACS). Emphasizes regional reperfusion strategies, hub-and-spoke PCI networks with 24/7 PCI capability, rapid fibrinolysis when transfer delays prevent timely PCI, and recommendations on EMS activation and ECG monitoring at first medical contact (FMC).

points: Primary care clinicians (general practitioners) can play an important early-care role for suspected ACS and may provide FMC in some countries.
Education and training in emergency, pre-hospital care for general practitioners is essential.
In many settings consulting a general practitioner instead of calling EMS increases pre-hospital delay; the public should be educated to call EMS directly for symptoms suggestive of ACS.

recommendations: Establish a regional reperfusion strategy to maximize efficiency of care for patients with a working diagnosis of STEMI.
Implement networks between hospitals (hub-and-spoke model) linked by prioritized and efficient ambulance services.
PCI centres should provide emergency invasive management 24/7 for suspected STEMI and offer intensive care, advanced cardiothoracic services, advanced haemodynamic support, and surgery as needed.
EMS should transport patients with a working diagnosis of STEMI to hospitals with a 24/7 PCI service, bypassing non-PCI-capable hospitals when possible.

Where transfer times to a primary PCI centre make recommended delays unachievable, develop protocols for rapid fibrinolysis at the place of STEMI diagnosis aiming for treatment within 10 minutes of FMC, followed by immediate transfer to a 24/7 PCI centre.
goals: Provide optimal care while minimizing delays to improve clinical outcomes.
Increase proportion of patients receiving reperfusion with the shortest possible treatment delay.
Measure and report quality of care, time delays, and patient outcomes to healthcare professionals contributing to EMS.
references: Further supplementary data referenced in guideline

points: Management of ACS starts at FMC when a working diagnosis of ACS is established.
Working diagnosis is usually based on symptoms consistent with myocardial ischaemia and signs on a 12-lead ECG.
It is recommended to initiate ECG monitoring at FMC (see Section 3.2).
